‘I wish we had a donkey. We should all come on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and I—with my dear husband walking beside us. I really must speak to him about buying one. I consider a donkey almost essential in the country. However much a woman has to occupy her, she cannot always stay shut up at home. And very long walks, you know—in summer there is the dust, and in winter the mud.’

‘You won't find either between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and it is completely dry at present. Still, come on a donkey if you prefer. You can borrow Mrs. Cole's. I should like everything to suit you as much as possible.’

‘I'm quite sure you would. Indeed, my good friend, I give you full credit. Beneath that rather dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are such an amusingly odd fellow. Yes, believe me, Knightley, I fully appreciate the consideration you have shown me in arranging all this. You have chosen the very thing to please me.’

Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding a table outdoors in the shade. He hoped to persuade Mr. Woodhouse to join the party along with Emma. He knew that seeing any of them sit outside to eat would inevitably make Mr. Woodhouse ill. He must not be lured into misery by the innocent-sounding offer of a morning drive and an hour or two at Donwell.

The invitation was honest. No hidden horrors would punish him for trusting it. He agreed to come. He had not visited Donwell for two years. ‘On some very fine morning, he and Emma and Harriet could manage the trip perfectly well. He could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked around the gardens. He supposed they could not be damp now, in the middle of the day. He would very much like to see the old house again, and would be delighted to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton and any of his other neighbours. He could see no objection at all to his going there with Emma and Harriet on some very fine morning. It was very good of Mr. Knightley to invite them—very kind and sensible—much more sensible than going out to dinner. He did not enjoy dining out.’

Mr. Knightley was fortunate: everyone agreed at once. The invitation was so warmly received that they all seemed, like Mrs. Elton, to regard the plan as a special compliment to themselves. Emma and Harriet said they expected to enjoy it immensely. Without being asked, Mr. Weston promised to bring Frank over to join them if possible. This particular expression of approval and gratitude could well have been spared. Mr. Knightley now had to say he would be glad to see Frank, and Mr. Weston promised to write immediately and use every argument he could to persuade him to come.

He chose Friday, August 17, for his appearance and spent most of the day examining his wardrobe. At last he settled on a large floppy hat with a red feather, a burial sheet with frills at the neck and wrists, and a rusty dagger. Toward evening, heavy rain began to fall, and the wind shook and rattled every door and window in the old house. It was exactly the kind of weather he enjoyed. His plan was to slip quietly into Washington Otis's room, jabber wildly at him from the end of the bed, and stab himself three times in the throat to slow music. He especially resented Washington, knowing perfectly well that the young man kept removing the famous Canterville bloodstain with Pinkerton's Paragon Detergent. Once he had terrified this reckless, foolish youth completely, he would enter the room shared by the American Minister and his wife. There he would press a cold, damp hand to Mrs. Otis's forehead while hissing the terrible secrets of the burial vault into her trembling husband's ear. He had not quite decided what to do about little Virginia. She had never insulted him, and she was pretty and gentle. He thought a few deep groans from the wardrobe would be more than enough. If those did not wake her, he could claw at her bedspread with fingers shaking uncontrollably. As for the twins, he was determined to teach them a lesson. First, of course, he would sit on their chests to give them the suffocating feeling of a nightmare. Their beds stood quite close together, so he would then stand between them as a green, ice-cold corpse until they were frozen with terror. Finally, he would cast off the burial sheet and crawl around the room, displaying his bleached white bones and one rolling eyeball, in the role of ‘Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide's Skeleton.’ He had performed this part with great success on several occasions, and considered it every bit as good as his celebrated ‘Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.’

At ten thirty he heard the family going to bed. For a while the twins disturbed him with loud shrieks of laughter. They were clearly entertaining themselves before settling down, with the carefree cheerfulness of schoolboys. By eleven fifteen, however, everything was quiet. When midnight struck, he set out. An owl beat against the windowpanes, a raven croaked in the old yew tree, and the wind roamed around the house, moaning like a lost soul. The Otis family slept on, unaware of the fate awaiting them. Above all the noise of the rain and storm, he could hear the steady snores of the Minister for the United States.

‘So now I own some knights,’ I said as we rode away. ‘Who would have guessed I'd live to put that sort of thing on a list of my assets? I won't know what to do with them, unless I hold a raffle. How many are there, Sandy?’

‘Seven, sir, if you please, and their squires.’

‘A good haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?’

‘Where do they hang out?’

‘Yes, where do they live?’

‘Ah, I did not understand you. I shall tell you shortly.’ Then, softly and thoughtfully, she began turning the words over on her tongue, savouring them: ‘Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out. Ah, yes, where do they hang out. Truly, the expression has a lovely charm, and the wording is delightful. I shall repeat it whenever I have a spare moment, so that perhaps I may learn it. Where do they hang out. Yes! It already comes easily to my tongue, and since—’

‘Don't forget the cowboys, Sandy.’

‘Cowboys?’

‘Yes, the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. A little while ago, remember? To put it another way, the game's begun.’

‘Game—’

‘Yes, yes, yes! Step up to bat. I mean, get on with the facts, and don't use up so much wood just getting your fire started. Tell me about the knights.’

‘Gladly, and I shall begin at once. So the two of them left and rode into a great forest. And—’

‘Good grief!’

You see, I understood my mistake immediately. I had set her machinery running, and it was my own fault. It would take her thirty days to reach the facts I wanted. Usually, she started without any introduction and finished without reaching a point. Interrupt her, and she would either continue without noticing or answer in a word or two, then repeat her last sentence. Interruptions only made things worse. Yet I had to interrupt, and fairly often, to save my life. Anyone would die with that monotonous voice dripping over them all day long.

‘Good grief!’ I exclaimed in desperation. She went straight back to the beginning:

‘So the two of them left and rode into a great forest. And—’

‘Which two?’

‘Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. They came to an abbey of monks and were comfortably housed there. In the morning they attended mass in the abbey, then rode on until they reached a great forest. There, in a valley beside a small tower, Sir Gawaine noticed twelve beautiful young ladies and two armed knights on large horses. The ladies were walking back and forth beside a tree.’
